https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.title: Duke of Westminster’s wedding: ‘most eligible bachelor’ gets married
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.text:
Two Just Stop Oil protesters have been arrested after apparently attempting to spoil the society wedding of the year.
The country’s richest person under 40, the seventh Duke of Westminster, today lost his unofficial title as Britain’s most eligible bachelor after he made Olivia Henson, 31, a duchess in front of 400 guests.
The ceremony at Chester Cathedral, which was attended by Prince William and Princess Eugenie, drew hundreds of people to celebrate on the city’s cobblestone streets. The number of Union Jacks being brandished made it reminiscent of a royal wedding.
However, not everyone gathered was a well-wisher. Hugh Grosvenor, 33, had just stepped out of the cathedral and kissed his new bride when two women who had been sitting peacefully by the barriers since the early hours of the morning released clouds of pressurised orange powdered paint, prompting boos from the crowd.
A local woman who had been standing next to the protesters all morning, Joanne Finnigan, 60, described the alleged stunt as “spiteful”, adding: “I don’t think anybody agreed with her at all. What does it prove? It doesn’t prove anything.”
Just Stop Oil quickly claimed responsibility for the protest.
“What do we value most? The wealth of billionaires like the Duke of Westminster or the lives of the billions who are being destroyed by the fossil fuel industry? Extreme wealth and the climate crisis are both symptoms of a broken system that is not serving most ordinary people,” a statement read.
A spokesman for Cheshire Constabulary confirmed that the two women were “quickly arrested on suspicion of public order offences” after letting off “a coloured flare”.
According to The Sunday Times Rich List, Grosvenor is the 14th richest person in the UK. He was 25 when he inherited his father’s £10.1 billion fortune after the late duke died suddenly aged 64 from a heart attack. Grosvenor’s 21st birthday party is thought to have cost £5 million.
The duke had arrived at the Cathedral in the morning in a Land Rover, accompanied by his three best men, all of whom are understood to be long-term friends.
Henson, an accounts manager at a food company, stepped out of a vintage Bentley with her father Rupert.
She was wearing a long-sleeved ivory silk dress with a keyhole back and hand-drawn veil by the British bridal designer Emma Victoria Payne, along with a tiara which has been in the Grosvenor family since 1906. She carried a bouquet of flowers picked from the gardens of Eaton Hall, the Grosvenor estate, comprising meadow grass, ox eye daisies, iris, rose, clematis, mock orange, scabious, sweet pea, astrantia, martagon lily and love in a mist.
The bride had to negotiate strong winds that played havoc with her waterfall veil — which was inspired by the one worn by her great-great-grandmother around 1880. Payne, a favourite designer of the Chelsea set, tried to hold it in place.
Prince William served as an usher to his old friend; however, Grosvenor’s other close confidant Prince Harry was nowhere to be seen, reportedly declining his invitation to avoid family tensions overshadowing the day. The Sussexes’ absence was particularly notable as Grosvenor is godfather to their son, Prince Archie, five.
The duke is also godfather to Prince George, ten, while his own godfather is the King.
Princess Eugenie, who wore an olive pleated dress and cream fascinator, was the only other member of the Royal Family seen in attendance. The Princess of Wales, who is continuing her recovery after revealing this year that she is undergoing chemotherapy, did not attend. Nor did the King who is also being treated for cancer and has just returned from the 80th anniversary commemoration of the D-Day landings in Normandy.
The Dean of Chester, the Very Rev Dr Tim Stratford, officiated the wedding, while the Bishop of Chester, the Right Rev Mark Tanner, preached. The service was in modern English, which Stratford said reflected the “contemporary couple”.
The newlyweds left the Cathedral around 1pm and were greeted by cheers of “hip, hip, hooray” as they kissed outside.
The Prince of Wales was seen chatting to other guests outside before they all drove off to attend an “intimate gathering” at nearby Eaton Hall, which has been in the Grosvenor family since the 1400s. The couple will be moving from London to live as a married couple in Chester, which the Duke described as “a really easy decision in the end”.
“They’re all really lovely people, they shop in all the local superstores, they’re very down to earth,” said Finnigan. “My children went to the school on their estate and any big events, such as bonfire night or anything, they’d invite all of the children.”
The duke gave 100,000 flowers to the city before the big day and has provided free ice cream for residents at three parlours across Chester. Seasonal flowers for the ceremony, which were sourced from local growers, will be made into bouquets after the wedding to be delivered to local charities, churches and organisations.
The duke, a former student of countryside management at Newcastle University, has three siblings: two older sisters, Lady Tamara and Lady Edwina, and one younger sister, Lady Viola. He inherited the estate as the oldest male heir.
Henson works at Belazu, based in London, which specialises in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern food products. She was introduced to the duke through mutual friends. She is widely reported to have studied at Marlborough College, where the Princess of Wales and Pippa Middleton, her sister, were educated.
When the new Duke and Duchess of Westminster released their engagement photo in April last year, it stood out to style commentators for the fact it was so relaxed — rather than an Instagram friendly blow-dry or new outfit, the smiling bride-to-be posed with minimal make-up, un-coiffed hair and a casual top and trousers.
Perhaps it is no surprise, then, that on her wedding day 31-year-old Olivia Henson kept things equally simple. Well, by society wedding standards, that is.
Not for her an aisle-wide poofy meringue, a statuesque silhouette, or several layers of tulle. For her nuptials, Henson chose a beautiful, minimal silk crepe satin slip dress with lace edging and a delicate floor-length veil.
The bespoke look was unpretentious, elegant and proof that the new Duchess is quite unbothered by flashy designer labels. The understated gown was the work of the London-based bridal designer Emma Victoria Payne, whose boutique atelier is based at Beauchamp Place in Chelsea.
It featured a bias cut skirt, pleated waistband and gathered sleeves that offered subtle volume at the top of each shoulder. The neckline came scalloped and edged — like the sleeves — with lace.
On the back of the dress the border of an oval-shaped cut-out got the same pretty treatment. Other details on the rear included a dropped waist, neat button detailing and a detachable two-metre train. No doubt this attachment was designed to be removed when she hit the dance floor at her reception.
The ensemble had several touching details sewn in. The dress incorporated floral motifs and edgings from the Duchesses’ great-great-grandmother’s veil. Henson’s own veil was embroidered with an original motif inspired by her engagement ring, as well as her own and the groom’s initials and wedding date.
Two other key accessories stood out. How many brides this summer might wish they had access to a show-stopping Fabergé myrtle leaf tiara? The one that sat atop the bride’s head today was a Grosvenor family heirloom and was created in 1906.
As for her statement “something-blue” shoes — which on-lookers got a flash of as she stepped out of the vintage Bentley — the velvet, bow-detail block heels are £343 from the Barcelona-based brand Silvia Lago.
Some 400 guests attended the ceremony. Each took a leaf out of the new Duchess’s book: generally, looks were polished but pared back.
Low-key headbands and hatinators took precedence over grand headwear. Princess Eugenie chose a cream veiled style to go with her olive-hued knit midi dress, which came with a pleated asymmetric skirt. She arrived with the former British Vogue editor Lady Violet Vestey, who wore a monochrome tweed two-piece skirt suit.
Mother of the groom, the Dowager Duchess of Westminster Natalia Grosvenor, opted for a fuss-free fuschia coat dress paired with a statement fascinator, classic red Maysale suede heels by Manolo Blahnik and a £1,578 “C’est quoi l’amour” clutch bag by handbag designer Olympia Le-Tan.
Her daughter, Lady Edwina Snow — who is goddaughter of the late Diana, Princess of Wales — was in a blush pink midi dress by the London-based label Roksanda.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Are we moving too fast towards net zero? The Sunday Times debate
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: Each week until polling day, two leading figures go head to head on the issues shaping Britain. Today Dominic Lawson and Dale Vince discuss Labour’s green goal
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Age: 62
Job: Green energy campaigner
Answer in a sentence: We’re not moving fast enough, not just from a climate perspective but from an economic one. The green economy is the biggest growth opportunity since the Industrial Revolution, which Britain led, against the naysaying of the Luddites of the day.
Age: 67
Job: Author and columnist
Answer in a sentence: Not yet; but Labour wants to accelerate into the next bend at 100mph and will crash the (electric) car.
Vince: Labour is talking about 100 per cent green energy on the grid by 2030. I think that’s very ambitious. But in broad terms super-ambitious targets are good, provided they’re feasible. And this one is. In business you’d call it a stretch target.
If we only get to 90 per cent by 2030, we’ll have achieved a lot, because we’re at 40-odd per cent green energy on the grid right now. It’ll take big, bold decisions on planning reform. For starters, we’ll need to unwind the Tory ban on onshore wind. We also need to oblige grid companies, which are monopoly operators, to invest in grid upgrades — even if it means preventing them from taking dividends until they’ve built the infrastructure we need.
We need to declare that wind farms, solar farms and pylons are vitally important national infrastructure and put them into a completely different planning regime where there’s a presumption in favour of them happening.
Lawson: Anything about election pledges is a political question. And purely in that sense Labour is right, as it wants to demonstrate that it is more concerned than the wicked Tories are about making Sir David Attenborough happy as he heads towards his 100th birthday in 2026. And Labour also will feel the pledge is useful in defending against encroachment on its vote from the Green Party.
Vince: I believe so, yes. The Tories have already changed the planning system once, but they did it to ban onshore wind. One of the big problems we have is that cuts to local authority budgets mean planning departments are smaller. We could take some decisions out of the hands of district councils, which are overwhelmed with work and underfunded, and centralise them to make faster decisions.
Onshore wind could be a game-changer. And we could use Labour’s proposed state-owned company, Great British Energy, to champion new technology that the private sector won’t yet back, such as tidal power. Great British Energy could also kick-start a national solar panel rooftop programme, bringing the benefits of clean energy directly to households.
Lawson: No, it is completely unrealistic: I credit Labour’s front bench with enough collective intelligence to know that. This month Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Britain’s most successful entrepreneur (in terms of wealth accumulated), declared that the idea it could be done by 2030 was “absurd”: this, from a man who the same week said he was backing Labour.
And among the party’s more traditional supporters, Gary Smith, the head of the GMB union — which represents many gas workers — has said of the plan, which would involve massive investment in undersea cables from France: “I don’t even worry about it. It cannot be done. There are four suppliers of [undersea] cables in the globe. They’re all booked out to 2030.”
In fact a scheme for an interconnector from Normandy to Portsmouth, which applied for planning permission in 2019, is still waiting for approval — held up for five years because of environmental objections by Portsmouth residents. Wait till a Labour government comes up against campaigns across the country over the building of five times as many transmission lines — pylons, in plain English — as have been constructed in the past 30 years.
Vince: I don’t think it needs to be costly: we don’t need public money for onshore wind and solar, which is fantastic. Investors are ready and waiting to build these things.
In terms of the upheaval it may bring, we all have to make sacrifices. Some people live next to a road or an airport. And we all have the benefit of that infrastructure as a shared asset. The fact is we need to expand certain infrastructure to bring our energy bills down and achieve energy security. These are really important national objectives. And I think they outweigh somebody’s objection based on the view that it might ruin the countryside.
I’d be very reluctant to start offering money off bills to sweeten the pill of having new pylons or a wind turbine by your house. Why single out energy for that kind of treatment? What about if a new road or a new school were built next door? Where do you draw the line?
We need to keep making the case for why we must decarbonise the grid and hit net zero by 2050, which is a legally binding agreement. Look at the energy crisis in 2022, when average bills were £4,000 a year. If we do this right, we’ll never have energy bills like that again. We’ll nail them to the floor. That’s a powerful argument for most people.
Lawson: Not “could be” very costly. Will be. The shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, Darren Jones, was recorded saying that the £28 billion Labour originally allocated to its Green Investment Plan — before realising it would make its claims it would not put up taxes completely incredible — was a “tiny amount” compared with what the 2030 plan would require. He said the real cost would be “hundreds of billions”. Or, as the head of Mitsubishi Power, Javier Colada, said last week, when asked about the 2030 pledge: “That would be a speed that I have never seen anywhere else.” And he added: “Is everyone so wealthy and so happy to increase the cost of everything?”
Labour claims that, when all the pylons and interconnectors are up and running, the day-to-day costs of electricity supply would be lower. But the reason wind turbine companies refused to take part in the government’s last auction of North Sea wind power licences was that, because of their increased costs, they couldn’t make a sufficient return, or at least not unless they were allowed to charge much higher prices in perpetuity. And tidal power — which has the great advantage, unlike wind, of not being intermittent — is many times more expensive: a 2019 study by the US Department of Energy found that commercial tidal energy projects cost up to $280 per megawatt hour, more than ten times as much as wind power. Labour, as the Conservatives do with their own 2035 plan, claims these “clean energy” investments will “pay for themselves”. Listen instead to Britain’s most respected energy economist, Sir Dieter Helm of Oxford University: “The trouble with this argument is that it simply is not true. No amount of assumptions to this effect make the models and predictions credible.”
Vince: Yes. But if we don’t do it ourselves, then we’ve got no voice to be lecturing others. People will say the UK only accounts for 1 per cent of global emissions, but that’s to overlook our historical carbon debt. We started the Industrial Revolution — we began this climate crisis.
It’s easy to point fingers at China, which is building new coal power stations. But it is also building wind and solar like there’s no tomorrow, and it is decarbonising its grid. It’s in a transition, but it’s ahead of us in making that transition. We have to get our house in order for our own sake, as well as for the world.
Lawson: Well, it’s a tempting idea, given the UK produces barely 1 per cent of global anthropogenic carbon emissions. Meanwhile, China and India are still constructing new coal-fired power stations, and have refused to give a date when they will stop generating energy from the stuff, which we have now completely removed from our own power supply. But what do you think China and India would say if we “put pressure on” them? Something like: you are not our masters now — beat it. Still, I suppose Just Stop Oil could send some of its hardiest demonstrators to Beijing to harangue the Chinese politburo. That would be entertaining.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: Supreme Court oil ruling: old schism rears its ugly head
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
Climate change presents a real challenge to modern democracies. No one can doubt the urgency of dealing with greenhouse gas emissions. However, governments have to consider the impact on whole populations that have built their lives on past assumptions about the availability of energy.
Measures to reduce demand for fossil fuels have a significant effect on people’s lives, and they are objecting in growing numbers. They need to heat their homes, get to work, take their children to school, run their businesses and so on. Many live on tight budgets. In the UK, France, the Netherlands and elsewhere, governments are retreating from earlier targets in the face of a backlash from voters.
In response campaigners have switched from attempts at demand management to the supply side. Groups such as Just Stop Oil hope to reduce production in Britain on the controversial assumption that big Middle Eastern, American and Russian producers will not fill the gap and that scarcity and rising prices will choke off consumption.
The UK Supreme Court’s latest pronouncement on the subject in last week’s ruling involving Surrey county council is a more cerebral version of the same idea. It also illustrates the growing appetite of judges in Britain and across Europe for stepping into this minefield by imposing rules that they consider necessary but might not command democratic support.
The case centred on a planning application to expand oil production at an existing onshore well site at Horse Hill. Planning authorities dealing with oil extraction projects must require and consider an environmental impact assessment.
Normally this will assess the impact of the operations at the site for which planning consent is being sought. This will include the emissions generated by the extraction process itself. That was all that the High Court and the Court of Appeal thought was necessary.
The Supreme Court disagreed. By a three to two majority the judges said that Surrey county council was required to consider not just the environmental impact of operations at the site, but also the environmental impact that the oil extracted would have on climate change more broadly: in other words, once it had left the site to be refined and burnt anywhere in the world.
Successive reports of the UN environment programme have argued that the current plans of the world’s governments envisage the extraction of more than twice the quantity of fossil fuels than would be consistent with keeping global warming to 1.5C. Surrey county council ought, they held, to have considered the contribution of Horse Hill to this state of affairs.
This has enormous implications for climate change policy. Most planning applications are dealt with by local authorities because they are best placed to assess the local implications. The Supreme Court’s decision means that any of Britain’s 324 local planning authorities may have to consider not just the local implications but also where the balance lies between national economic objectives and the reduction of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Each of them will have their own, inconsistent, policies. But Lord Leggatt, delivering the majority judgment, leaves little doubt where he would draw the balance, forcefully arguing the case for drastic limitations on the UK’s fossil fuel extraction.
The problem about this — as Lord Sales points out in his powerful dissent — is that in a field that cries out for coherent policy-making, the majority’s answer is incoherent. The real issue in the case was not what to do about climate change, but who is to decide what to do about climate change.
The impact on global climate change of refining and burning oil worldwide is a matter of national and international policy. Climate change targets are set internationally by treaty. Measures to achieve them are matters for national policy, governed in Britain by the Climate Change Act 2008 and the licensing scheme of the Petroleum Act 1998.
Ministers perform this function by looking at Britain as a whole. This may involve allowing more development in some regions or some sectors of the economy and less in others.
There is an obvious case for dealing with these issues at national and international levels. There is no case at all for dealing with it at the level of a local authority answerable only to the residents of Surrey. Local planning committees are neither constitutionally charged with such a task nor competent to perform it.
The decision looks like a re-emergence of the old schism in the Supreme Court between those who were concerned primarily with the proper distribution of constitutional functions, and judicial activists who were more interested in influencing the substance of policy. It would be unfortunate if this became the pattern of the future.
One of the problems with the old schism was that there were too many cases in which one felt that the result might have gone the other way with a differently constituted panel. This was and is bad for the authority and reputation of the court. It may in future be necessary for it to sit more often in enlarged panels, especially on cases with important implications for national policy.
Lord Sumption is a former justice of the Supreme Court

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.title: Wimbledon ‘hopeful’ Princess of Wales will present trophies
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.subtitle: The All England Club chairwoman, Debbie Jevans, said they will give Kate ‘as much flexibility as possible’ as she continues her cancer treatment
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.text:
Kensington Palace has not ruled out the possibility of the Princess of Wales presenting the trophies at Wimbledon, as planned, as she continues to undergo cancer treatment.
Organisers remain “hopeful” that Kate might attend to present the honours to the men’s and women’s singles winners.
She is the patron of the All England Lawn Tennis Club and would usually be expected to present trophies to the men’s and ladies’ singles winners. But there was some doubt about how her schedule would change after she revealed her cancer diagnosis in March.
Wimbledon’s organisers remain optimistic the princess will return to the royal box after she featured at the Trooping the Colour ceremony, her first public appearance since she released a video statement disclosing her condition.
Debbie Jevans, chairwoman of the All England Club, told Telegraph Sport they would give Kate “as much flexibility as possible” as she continued her treatment and may decide who will present the trophies on the morning of the finals.
She said: “We’re hopeful that the Princess of Wales will be able to present the trophies as the club’s patron, but her health and recovery is the priority.
“I don’t know who would present the trophies as an alternative — that’s something to consider nearer the time if necessary. We’re staying flexible. When we hear, we’ll then think about what’s the right thing to do.”
The princess said before the Trooping of the Colour that she has “good days and bad days” with her treatment.
“On those bad days you feel weak, tired and you have to give in to your body resting. But on the good days, when you feel stronger, you want to make the most of feeling well,” she said.
Royal sources indicated to the paper that Kate would like to attend Wimbledon if possible. Options to replace her if she is unable to include another member of the royal family or Jevans, as chairwoman of the club, and a former Wimbledon player.
Last year, Kate presented the trophy to Czech Marketa Vondrousova, after she defeated Ons Jabeur in straight sets to become the first unseeded player to win the Wimbledon women’s single title.
The princess — herself a keen tennis player and fan of the game — consoled the tearful Jabeur, who described the defeat as the “most painful loss of my career”, with a hug. Kate received the role of Wimbledon patron when Queen Elizabeth II, after holding the role for 64 years, handed it over in 2016.
Since her appointment, Kate has often been spotted with her family in the royal box, sitting with the likes of Roger Federer and Daniel Craig. She attracted headlines when she attended the tournament with the Duchess of Sussex in 2018 to watch the women’s singles final, their first official engagement without their husbands.
Separately, jigsaw puzzles have been withdrawn from sale at Wimbledon after climate protesters used them to circumvent a massive security operation and disrupt play at last year’s tournament. Activists from Just Stop Oil interrupted two matches by marauding on to courts and throwing orange confetti that had been hidden inside jigsaw boxes.
The disruption took place despite a significantly heightened security at the All England Club following a spate of similar stunts by the group at major sporting events.
The Just Stop Oil protesters each used a 1,000-piece jigsaw puzzle called Centre Court View, launched for the centenary celebrations in 2022, featuring Federer mid-serve, that had been purchased on the grounds. Wimbledon’s shop first appeared to halt sales of the £22 puzzle in the immediate aftermath of the protests and they will not be available to visitors on site this year.
However, a jigsaw featuring Wimbledon’s trophies on Centre Court can be bought from Wimbledon’s online shop.
A club spokesman said: “The safety and security of all our visitors is paramount. Throughout the year we work closely with the Metropolitan Police and other relevant organisations to ensure that the championships is as safe and secure as possible and that our plans and measures are commensurate with the threat level and prevailing risks.
“We ask that all visitors to the championships respect the safety and enjoyment of all guests who are in attendance.”

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: What Greenpeace learnt in Russia — don’t mess with Putin
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
On Thin Ice: Putin v GreenpeaceBBC2Presumed InnocentApple TV+Inside No 9BBC2
One enticing thing about making climate villains out of book festivals, I suppose, is that a book festival is unlikely to blast you with a water cannon and try to knock you into the Arctic ocean. Nor will a book festival pull a gun on you or throw you in jail and threaten to keep you there for a decent chunk of the rest of your life. Although one strong lesson of On Thin Ice: Putin v Greenpeace was that book festivals might have a much easier time of it if they did.
This was a documentary about the 2013 Greenpeace operation to hinder production on the Russian Prirazlomnaya oil rig, way up in the Arctic Circle where the northern lights flash and the bears all wear armour. At heart, this fascinating six-part documentary was really a story of naivety. Most of this was on the part of the crew of the Arctic Sunrise, and their support organisation back home, who seemed to have assumed that the Russian authorities would treat hippy climate protesters much as, say, the Norwegian ones do.
At first, I wondered if there was Russian naivety on display here, too, as a variety of coastguards, soldiers and miscellaneous thugs met the crew with exactly the sort of heavy-handed militaristic response that western governments are at pains, particularly when the cameras are rolling, to avoid. Gradually, though, it became plain that the Russians had done none of this by mistake. They just didn’t give a toss.
Early on, as the Arctic Sunrise’s de facto commander Frank Hewetson put it, the plan “went to shit”. Activists ended up scaling the sides of the rig while workers above hosed them down, and soldiers below pointed guns at them. They were lucky, clearly, that nobody drowned or was shot. Instead, their boat was stormed, in breach of international law, and they ended up on trial in Moscow, facing up to 15 years in jail. “I thought they’d hold us for a couple of days!” people kept saying, as if they had expected Vladimir Putin to be more like, you know, Nick Clegg.
As well as being naive, Greenpeace was also chaotic. As the boat was stormed, a crew member managed to call back to London to speak to Ben Stewart, the group’s head of media. He was drunk in a nightclub. In the subsequent days his primary concern seems to have been what hashtag to use online to publicise the case. “#FreeTheSunrise30,” he mused. “Sounds like a vitamin pill.” He also spoke to the BBC’s veteran Russian expert Martin Sixsmith to get a sense of what Russia might do. Now? Now you do this?
Later, his team came up with a media-grabbing plan for Kumi Naidoo, the head of Greenpeace, to offer himself to be jailed in Russia in exchange for the crew. “We’d better ask Kumi about this,” Stewart reported them belatedly saying. All of this was perhaps less endearing than he imagined.
• Read more of Hugo Rifkind’s content for The Times
Meanwhile, the crew were languishing in cells. I remember the period well because one of those being held was a young journalist who until recently had been working for The Times. I also remember the agonised debates in the office about whether we should be publicising this or not; whether it would help or actually do the opposite. Greenpeace should have seen all of this coming. There wasn’t much sign that it had.
I remain in awe of anyone prepared to risk life or liberty for a cause like this. Bits of the dynamic, though, continue to nag. Clearly activists expected, as westerners, to be treated differently, no matter that the bulk of their protests beforehand had been levelled at the west. Clearly also, in a direct reverse of that point, they were being fêted as heroes by most western governments, no matter that the most famous Greenpeace ship before the Arctic Sunrise was the Rainbow Warrior, which was sunk by the French. Hypocrisy abounded. I’m not sure if, excellent as it was, this documentary acknowledged much of that.
The Russians, by contrast, were pitiless in clarity. “Protest us,” the message was, “and you will suffer.” Only towards the end of this series did anybody begin to acknowledge that, actually, Greenpeace might have done the Kremlin a favour. Arctic drilling continues to this day. And, as one activist put it, “I don’t think anyone has protested a Russian oil rig since.”
Presumed Innocent is a new TV version of the film from 1990, fondly remembered for what Harrison Ford and Greta Scacchi did on a desk. Although for anyone of about my age, it ranks up there with Jagged Edge, Fatal Attraction, Indecent Proposal, Basic Instinct and a bunch of other films with two-word titles as one of the reasons why we all grew up faintly worrying that sex itself was a bad idea and probably a forerunner to being horrifically murdered, probably by somebody in a balaclava.
Jake Gyllenhaal plays the Ford role, and only sometimes looks like he’s playing Ford playing it. For those who forget, this is the story of a Chicago prosecutor (Rusty Sabich, Gyllenhaal) whose colleague is murdered. They were having an affair, and the murder resembles one from a case they tried together. Before long, this puts him in the dock. The victim here is Carolyn Polhemus, played by Renate Reinsve. She’s present mainly in flashbacks, largely nude or dead.
The backdrop is political. Sabich has recently lost his role as deputy prosecutor after his former boss Raymond Horgan (Bill Camp) lost an election to the smooth Nico Della Guardia (O-T Fagbenle), who has his own attack dog in the shape of Peter Sarsgaard’s Tommy Molto. Now on the stand, Sabich is being defended by Horgan and prosecuted by the other two, which is neat.
Two episodes in, the best thing about Presumed Innocent is how accurately it really does recreate the sensation of settling down in front of one of those long, tense, crackingly good Hollywood thrillers of 30-plus years ago. The moment you realise that, though, you may begin to ask yourself why you’re not just watching one.
Had it been made in the 1980s, 1990s or even early 2000s,Inside No 9would still be discussed in tones of awe, held up as an example of the sort of classic telly nobody makes any more. As a fixture of the streaming age, instead, it has always been merely quite a lot better than almost everything else. Or as Reece Shearsmith, playing himself, put it in the final episode this week: “These little half-hour nothings. Every fourth one a dud.”
I’m not sure I’ve ever seen a dud. Certainly some are better than others — the wordless one with burglars from the first series is a thing of beauty for ever and ever, and I also loved the karaoke one that other people didn’t — but they have never been bad, even on the terribly rare occasion you might have seen the twist coming. Either way, this week, after an inevitable nine seasons (albeit each with only six episodes, and over an irritatingly close ten years) it came to an end. The final episode — Plodding On — was funny and smart, yet not really much like Inside No 9 at all.
We were in a nightclub, at the show’s own wrap party. First we met Katherine Parkinson and Tim Key, awkwardly doing cocaine in the toilet. The conceit, generally, was that the show had ended and Shearsmith and his writing partner, Steve Pemberton, had fallen out. Shearsmith had pitched a new show to the BBC, but Pemberton was off to America for big bucks instead. Most of this came out via a pretend podcast interview conducted in the toilet by Nick Mohammed. Along the way you had vast swathes of the stars who have appeared on this show, from Conleth Hill to Mark Gatiss to Alison Steadman to Zoë Wanamaker and on and on. A thing you can only do when deeply loved.
I won’t tell you how it ended, except to say that if you aren’t a mega fan of the show then you probably won’t have quite understood it. This was a shame because for all the devotion it has inspired, the real brilliance of Inside No 9 has always been precisely that this wasn’t necessary, with every episode capable of working as a perfect self-contained whole. Still, it was sweet enough. I particularly liked the suggestion, made by Robin Askwith, that a future episode should have the twist that everyone is dead. “We’ve done that three times,” Shearsmith replied.
That I immediately thought, “Only three?” is a strength, not a weakness. Not just a show, this, but a genre. We’ll miss it.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: The Just Stop Oil Swiftie who tried to spray Taylor’s jet orange
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Protesters were said to have been targeting Taylor Swift’s private plane before her concerts at Wembley — but police confirm the aircraft was not there
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Jennifer Kowalski was overjoyed to meet Taylor Swift in 2015 when the star jetted into Glasgow on her sellout world tour, and smiled broadly as the chart-topping singer threw her arms around Kowalski and her sister for a photo. Nine years later, as Swift returned to Britain for her Eras Tour, Kowalski’s adoration has turned to abhorrence over the US superstar’s controversial use of private jets.On Thursday morning, Kowalski, 28, and a fellow Just Stop Oil activist, Cole Macdonald, 22, broke into a VIP section at Stansted airport and sprayed two private jets with orange paint, near to where Swift’s aircraft was believed to have been parked. A video showed the protesters using an angle grinder on the metal fence to gain access to the airfield in Essex shortly after 5am. The climate protest group, which has gained notoriety for its disruptive tactics, is demanding the government end all new oil and gas projects.Swift, whose hits include I Knew You Were Trouble, has been criticised by Chris Packham, the wildlife and environmental broadcaster and campaigner, for her “absurd” use of private planes. It has been reported that she racked up 178,000 miles on her two planes last year. A video posted on social media showed one activist targeting each aircraft, using a fire extinguisher filled with orange paint. The pair, who each wore white Just Stop Oil T-shirts, hugged each other after they defaced the jets.Speaking directly to the camera, they said: “We just spray-painted the f*** out of this private jet and the one behind.” Swift’s rented plane was not one of the jets damaged. Kowalski, a former sustainability manager from Dumbarton in central Scotland, said: “Over the years, I’ve had to realise that even working in sustainability provides me with essentially no ability to make the necessary changes to prevent the complete collapse of our natural systems. I have to take desperate measures to make my voice heard.”Macdonald, from Brighton, added: “We’re living in two worlds: one where billionaires live in luxury, able to fly in private jets away from the other, where unlivable conditions are being imposed on countless millions.”
Kowalski and Macdonald were arrested on suspicion of criminal damage and interference with the use or operation of national infrastructure and taken into custody.
Essex police said they were alerted to reports that two people had gained access to an area away from the runway and main passenger terminal. Officers were “on the scene within minutes” and the suspects were detained.
Simon Anslow, chief superintendent of Essex police said the force was not “anti-protest” but added that officers will “always take action where criminal acts take place”.
He added: “I would like to reassure passengers and the wider public that we are well prepared and resourced to deal with incidents of this nature. We maintain a constant presence at the airport and this presence will be heightened over the summer period. We have a good working relationship with Stansted Airport to ensure you can go about your travels with minimal impact.”
The police force said the airport and flights were operating as normal.
Just Stop Oil repeated its call for the next government to “sign up to a legally binding treaty to phase out fossil fuels by 2030”.
“Whilst governments are allowing oil corporations to run amok destroying our communities, the actions of individuals mean very little. Failure to defend the people they represent will mean Just Stop Oil supporters, along with citizens from Austria, Canada, Norway, the Netherlands and Switzerland will join in resistance this summer, if their own governments do not take meaningful action,” a spokesman said.
Swift becoming a target of Just Stop Oil will no doubt divide her fans, many of whom are devoted followers of her music and style. But as Swift’s musical output continues to break records and she delights millions of fans around the world on her sell-out tours, she has faced calls to abandon her use of private jets amid the climate crisis.
• Taylor Swift threatens to sue student who tracks celebrity private jets
Jack Sweeney, a university student from Florida, in the US, incurred the wrath of Swift over his TaylorSwiftJets social media account, which tracks the singer’s flights.
Her lawyers claimed that plane tracking was a “life-or-death matter” and there was “no legitimate interest in or public need for this information, other than to stalk, harass, and exert dominion and control”.
Sweeney, an aviation buff who is studying IT, told BBC News: “I was just kind of doing this as a hobby as I found it interesting. The flyers are trying to hide the bad PR of [carbon] emissions.”
Naturally, he shared a photo of his lawyer’s response to the legal threat with his followers. His Swiftian caption read: “Look What You Made Me Do”.

https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/fash.title: Vivienne Westwood’s wardrobe is up for sale at Christie’s
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/fash.text:
She’s the legendary anti-establishment designer from Derbyshire, whose lifelong activism was often as avant-garde as her clothes. Now Dame Vivienne Westwood’s biggest fans can own their own bit of her iconic wardrobe. They just need to place the highest bid.
From this weekend until June 28, Christie’s is exhibiting and selling 273 items of clothing and accessories from the so-called godmother of punk’s personal collection. The historic auction house in St James’s, London, has been taken over by Westwood fever.
Outside, the late designer’s name is lit up in neon huge neon pink cursive signage. On Friday morning queues to access the free exhibition started an hour before it opened to the public.
Sarah, a 49-year-old press officer for the British Film Institute who was first in line, described it as a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity”. She explained she had come to Christie’s to: “See stuff up close, to see what appealed to her [Westwood] personally. A person’s wardrobe says a lot about them.”
“I’ve always loved her work,” added Lorraine, 51, a fashion lecturer. “She’s always been honest — true to herself. It’s an honour [to be able to come here] — a way for people to show their appreciation of her work.”
The crowds had gathered to admire garments, jewellery and signature platform shoes that Westwood, who died aged 81-years-old in December 2022, herself owned and loved. Every piece on display at Christie’s is for sale. The estimated price of lots starts at £200, going as high as £50,000.
True to Westwood’s lifelong dedication to effecting change — though in a slightly more reserved manner than when she drove a white tank to No 10 to protest fracking in 2015 — all proceeds will be donated to four charities she spent her career working with: The Vivienne Foundation, Amnesty International, Médecins Sans Frontières and Greenpeace.
A cropped navy velvet jacket, styled over a pussybow blouse, will be an immediate draw to fashion buffs. It is the designer’s version of one Naomi Campbell wore when she famously fell over on Westwood’s Autumn 1993 runway — and estimated to sell for between £800 and £1,200.
A little black dress priced between £3,000 and 5,000, complete with cape and signature Westwood draping and dramatic silhouette, is what she wore to her investiture at Buckingham Palace in 2006. An emerald green duchess satin two-piece is £2,500 to £4,000; a suit in her vivid “Anglomania” tartan, which she added to the Scottish Register of Tartans in 1993, could go for £3,000.
Most impressive of all might be a regal, oyster-hued, taffeta corseted ball gown, priced between £5,000-£8,000. Such a frock would not be amiss on a Bridgerton set in 2024 but it is in fact what Westwood attended the opening of her V&A exhibition wearing, in 1998.
What else? Statement orb-strewn jewellery and platform heels are Westwood trademarks. But unexpected personal accessories come part of some lots, too. A few still have hand-drawn “CLIMATE REVOLUTION” badges pinned on. On the back of one skirt you can find a needle left in the seam, mid-mend.
There is just one article you couldn’t wear: a set of ten “playing card” prints by the designer. These are expected to fetch the highest price of all: up to £50,000. Punters can bid on most pieces online until June 28. Ninety-five standout items are being held back for a live sale taking place on June 25.
In an interview on the eve of its launching, Adrian Hume-Sayer, a director at Christie’s leading the sale, said that conversations began with Dame Westwood a year and a half ago — and that the idea of selling her wardrobe for charity was one she “fully supported”.
Since, the house has worked with Westwood’s widower, Andreas Kronthaler — who now runs her brand — to collate the expansive collection. The showcase is not just for hopeful punters, but a free public exhibition.
“We hope and expect that a lot of people will come who aren’t necessarily going to bid in the sale, but want to see these things because this is the only time they’ve ever been exhibited en masse,” explained Hume-Sayer, adding that, “when they’ve been sold, they will scatter”.
He predicts that items will be purchased by collectors and fans not just to keep vacuum packed or behind glass, but to wear. “This is what was hanging in her wardrobe, in her house. These are wearable things,” he explained.
Still, most visitors will likely only leave with one of the £25 canvas “stay punk” tote bags.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Why Starmer will struggle to deliver growth
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
The technical economic term is, I believe, a “no-brainer”. The exports stimulated by the Aukus defence pact, under which Britain will help Australia to build nuclear-powered submarines, promise to create thousands of skilled jobs and billions in long-term investment for one of our most deprived areas. All the government has to do is send a bit of extra funding to Barrow, the Cumbrian port town where BAE Systems will carry out much of the work. An easy decision, surely?
Ho, ho, ho! Let me introduce you, my friend, to His Majesty’s Treasury, home to the deranged Scrooges masquerading as experts in charge of the British economy. When Aukus was signed, local and central government officials speedily put together an application for £250 million in funding over a decade to pay for improvements to Barrow’s infrastructure, schools, training and health provision that would be needed to attract highly skilled people and train up local talent.
For context, the initial BAE contract to build the subs is worth £3.95 billion alone, which excludes all the knock-on economic benefits and further deals it will bring in over the decades.
• Iain Martin: Keir Starmer must put Aukus defence pact before Brussels
After a year — yes, a whole year — of wrangling, Treasury nit-picking, two widely publicised trips to Barrow by Michael Gove and a specially written letter of intervention to the prime minister and chancellor from the cabinet secretary himself, the Treasury grudgingly agreed to provide £200 million to enable the lucrative, security-critical project to go ahead. Job done, I suppose, but at what cost in bureaucratic talent, political capital and sheer wasted time?
When government outsiders like Rachel “I love the Treasury” Reeves wonder how certain rogue Tories could be so reckless as to start a war on the UK’s most powerful government department, they ought to look at cases like Barrow. The mavericks are not insane. The British state is deeply deficient and Britain is stagnating.
Yes, the Liz Truss-Kwasi Kwarteng regime was stunningly arrogant and administratively incompetent, but they were pursuing exactly what Reeves and Keir Starmer also say is their main mission: growth. Truss failed thanks to a massive, career-ending misjudgment. Labour is likely to fail over a longer period for different reasons.
It isn’t just the Starmer team’s misplaced faith in our mandarins that will thwart its aims. Labour’s problems are also ideological. Take the proposed Lower Thames Crossing, which has infamously produced Britain’s longest planning document at 359,000 pages. As the technical notes reveal, EU-derived regulations like the habitats directive are a primary reason for its astonishing length.
Starmer has promised to get things “built quicker and cheaper”, getting “shovels in the ground [and] cranes in the sky”. Yet he won the Labour leadership by courting support from the party’s most pro-European members and has since promised repeatedly not to diverge from or dilute EU-derived environmental standards. The only cranes in the sky favoured by this regime will be avian.
Neither Labour’s actions nor its manifesto have done anything to dispel this impression. The party voted to keep in place the current regime governing nutrient pollution, under which a powerful quango advised a halt to all new housebuilding in 74 local authority areas despite the negligible environmental impact.
The manifesto has little to say on the issue other than: “We will implement solutions to unlock the building of homes affected by nutrient neutrality without weakening environmental protections.” Gosh, I wonder why the Tories didn’t think of that.
As for energy policy, the party’s potentially growth-enhancing pledge of £28 billion in capital spending has fallen victim to pre-emptive Treasury doom-mongering — yet the economy-killing net zero targets are here to stay. This is exactly the policy mix pursued at such devastating cost by the Tories. In the war of Labour donors, with the Ecotricity owner and former Just Stop Oil funder Dale Vince squaring up to Unite, it’s the eco-warrior who’s won.
Unite has refused to endorse Labour’s manifesto because it crossed the union’s “red line” by failing to have any plan for the livelihoods of oil and gas workers. The ultimate victors are, again, the forces of economic stagnation.
This anti-growth coalition, as Truss correctly termed it, is usually the default winner across the country too. Look at the refusal of planning permission for Marlow Film Studios, a proposed £750 million movie-making hub on empty 1950s landfill next to a major A-road. The new studio, on a scale to rival some of the world’s biggest and best, promised to employ 2,000 people directly and create 2,000 more jobs in its supply chain, plus 600 training places and various amenities such as a bus to the Elizabeth Line in Maidenhead and a small wood.
Its planning assessment concluded that changes to a nearby roundabout would actually improve traffic on the main road. One of the fields on the site is apparently so adverse to life that, when a herd of horses was placed on it some years ago, two of them died. But, no matter. The land is designated as greenbelt. Permission denied.
Cases like this support the theory that the British economy is a “coiled spring”: a place of marvellous energy and dynamism if it weren’t constantly suppressed by political dysfunction and the dominance of favoured interest groups. Say what you like about Truss, but she wasn’t afraid to pick fights with such types.
Indeed, an eight-page policy document from her brief period in office contains some surprisingly plausible, if controversial, ideas to foster growth: allow homeowners automatic permission to build extensions or convert outbuildings in the way businesses and farms can; fast-track visas for graduates of particular courses at the world’s top 50 universities; make Covid-era outdoor dining permits permanent; and encourage the signing of long-term gas deals with US and Middle East suppliers. Truss might have lacked the competence to achieve any of this but Reeves and Starmer lack a different, no less critical ingredient: chutzpah.
It may be, of course, that the incoming Labour government will be the first to campaign in prose and govern with poetic licence. Perhaps a majority in the hundreds, falling interest rates and an already anticipated economic recovery will work in the government’s favour. But it will take more than good timing and civil service euphoria to shift Britain out of its rut.
Starmer has defined himself as the antithesis of Truss. But if, like her, he fails in his drive for growth, he may instead end up as her more boring doppelgänger.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: On Thin Ice: Putin v Greenpeace — gripping, blow-by-blow details
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.subtitle: Also reviewed: The Piano — The Final
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
On Thin Ice: Putin v GreenpeaceBBC2
The Piano: The FinalChannel 4
There aren’t many things that can make you more cross than when, say, climate-change protesters bring a motorway to a standstill while you’re in the slow lane. Yet, if pushed, it’s hard to disagree that nonviolent protest — annoying as it may be — is a potent way to make social change actually happen, at least in a nice democracy like ours. But what happens when they protest against a less fair-minded society? Against, indeed, a James Bond villain?
When they drew up their plan to scale a Russian oil rig, the activists on board Greenpeace’s ship the Arctic Sunrise didn’t factor into it the possibility that Vladimir Putin would be in the mood to strip off his shirt and show his country how tough he is. The subsequent plight of the crew sparked an international outcry in 2013, your memory of which will have come flooding back during On Thin Ice: Putin v Greenpeace, a perhaps unexpectedly gripping new blow-by-blow account.
Theirs was a peaceful if reckless protest but, as the Arctic Sunrise’s co-ordinator, Frank Hewetson, put it succinctly here: “The plan, I think you could say, went to shit.” The Russian coastguard forcibly took control of the boat and hauled them off to Murmansk, where they were slung into prison for “piracy”, each facing the distinct possibility of 15 years inside. They had accidentally wandered into a far bigger game.
Putin was on a mission of his own after the domestic unrest over his return to the presidency, and the “Arctic 30” had served themselves up as red meat for him to demonstrate to his people that he would defend the mother country. And with oil production being so essential to his government’s finances, an attack on his Gazprom drilling platform was, as a former company spokesman put it, “an attack on the Kremlin, an attack on Putin”.
The pacing of this series, which edits into six tidy half-hour episodes a mix of recollections and footage (some taken by the crew to place us right there in the thick of things), just doesn’t let up. It began with several of the activists describing why they were there in the first place, giving in just a few economical quotes an idea of who these people actually were.
One said that she had been working in marketing in Abu Dhabi — quite a contrast to anti-oil activism — before watching, horrified, the news footage of the BP oil spills in 2010. Another, an engineer on board, said: “I grew up sailing. I always liked books about sailing around the world.” What was his day job? “Mostly mending toilets.”
From there the contributors gave such a close-up account of all hell breaking loose — of Russians in balaclavas storming their ship, waving guns — that you could see why two of them separately suggest that it was “like finding yourself in the middle of a James Bond movie”. The vivid, edge-of-sofa details here for once made you feel that a movie version would be superfluous.★★★★☆
If the blub-inducing reality series The Piano has started to feel as much a contest of “most emotional backstory” as piano ability, last night’s final threatened to become the world’s first weeping competition. The seven piano pieces performed to a sold-out auditorium prompted reactions ranging from a dignified, wiped-away tear to screwed-up-face sobbing.
Each performer was a delight in their own distinct way (spoiler ahead), such that it felt almost unfair that anyone should win over anyone else. Still, I can’t see many arguing with the pick of Brad, looking like an early 1960s Beatle, as giving the performance of the night. A worthy winner and, as things ended in (yes) more tears, an undeniably lovely hour of TV.★★★★☆

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/photography-.title: Stonehenge and a summer solstice disrupted by hippies — in the archive
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/photography-.text:
The annual druids ceremony this year went ahead at Stonehenge as usual, a day after protesters from Just Stop Oil vandalised the prehistoric stones.
Traditionally the ceremony is one of the rare occasions where people can get up close to the stones, but disrespecting the monuments is nothing new. In 1984, the druids ceremony “was marred by crowds” as “hundreds of hippies” from a nearby music festival gatecrashed proceedings. Revellers from the Stonehenge Free Festival climbed onto the stones, disrupting the ceremony as they “sat smoking pot”.
As midsummer approached in 2024, Kate Spicer examined the rising appeal of the summer solstice soirée, from “parties to poetry readings” and “salutations at stone circles”.
The Sunday Times published a weekly feature leading up to polling day as two writers “go head to head on issues shaping Britain”. Robert Colvile and Terri White discussed the implications of Labour’s plans to end VAT breaks for private schools.
This photograph from 1937 shows the boys at Eton College relaxing in the reading room in between classes. Closer inspection of the image gives a glimpse of the publications being perused. The students enjoy a varied collection including Punch Magazine, Sporting Life, an unidentified tabloid newspaper and the broadsheet edition of The Times.
Two images taken in 1951 show a group of London schoolchildren departing for their Ipswich boarding school as their parents wave them off. The former stately home at Woolverstone Hall was purchased by London county council that year, providing a sliding scale of paid education for London boys. Eleven-year-old Anthony Jones from Putney is photographed excitedly waving farewell to his curious younger brother Allan.
Constance Kampfner reported from Clacton-on-Sea, where Nigel Farage announced his political comeback. Recently named “Britain’s joint least-favourite seaside resort”, the Essex town is home to “the third highest proportion of economically inactive people in the country”. However, these images show Clacton in the 1950s was the go-to destination. A gathering in 1950 of the Young Conservatives, who assembled in front of the pier before the conference, was organised by Lord Mancroft.
Farage attracted crowds to the same location to speak of his parliamentary aspirations, but in 1951 it was the Punch and Judy show not politics that drew in the hordes. This atmospheric image captures a packed scene as “a solid mass of children and adults” cram in like sardines for the traditional holiday entertainment.
On the 80th anniversary of the Normandy landings, Jack Blackburn’s live blog recreated “D-Day as it happened: how the Allied landings unfolded in real time”.
Some of the heroes from that historic operation were photographed in the subsequent years. Major John Howard of ‘D’ Company 2nd Battalion Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry returned to those Normandy beaches three years later with his wife and children. David Johnson photographed them visiting Pegasus Bridge, where Howard led the glider-borne assault. Stopping next at Ranville Churchyard they paid their respects to the grave of Lieutenant Den Brotheridge, the first Allied soldier killed in action that day. A poignant moment captures an everyday familiar scene as Howard, with his trousers rolled up, holds hands with his children as they run along the beach, feeling the sand between their toes.
Ernest Shackleton’s ship, Quest, was finally located after sinking in the ice 62 years ago. The steamship used for Shackleton’s last voyage (on which the explorer died of a heart attack in 1922) was discovered on the 150th anniversary of his birth by the Royal Canadian Geographical Society.
This image shows the ship passing under Tower Bridge to be fitted out before the Shackleton-Rowett expedition. Another photograph captured crew member Bee Mason, the official photographer to the voyage. Mason was one of two crew members sent home due to chronic sea sickness. Weeks later The Times reported as Quest left St Katharine Docks to set sail on its “30,000 mile voyage of discovery”.
This month members of the Sikh community marched through central London in protest over the storming of India’s Golden Temple 30 years ago. In 1984 The Times reported from Delhi with the headline: “Sikhs stunned by Amritsar temple violation and number of deaths”. Days later a major demonstration was held as 25,000 Sikhs marched through London. John Voos captured a scene of “Sikhs and swords in a peaceful London protest”. Thirty years later the marches continue, as they still demand the truth and that the tragic events of Operation Blue Star be recognised as a genocide. In 2017 Ben Macintyre reported on the “Golden Temple’s long-buried secrets’’.
Demis Hassabis, chief executive of DeepMind, “was a 12-year-old at a north London comprehensive when he decided to devote his life to artificial intelligence”. Matthew Syed met “Britain’s deepest mind”. Hassabis is the subject of a new film, The Thinking Game, which premiered this month at the Tribeca Festival in New York. It chronicles his company’s race toward “creating the smartest machine in the world in the AI space race”. The film uncovered images of Hassabis as a seven-year-old chess prodigy, photographed by John Voos, while competing in the London Junior Chess Championships and “pondering his next move”. Five years later Marc Aspland photographed a smiling Hassabis at another competition in this previously unpublished shoot.
Paul McCartney celebrated turning 82 by announcing new dates for his Got Back world tour. With the former Beatle at an age “when many people might be tempted to put their feet up”, Pete Bee asked: “How does he do it?” Frank Herrmann photographed McCartney for The Sunday Times in 1973 for the article “Taking off with Linda”. Wings had just released their album Red Red Speedway to a lukewarm critical response. Linda was unperturbed: “Whatever the critics say, the people like us.” This seemed justified as they pushed ahead with a “triumphal British tour”. Only one photo from the shoot was ever published, these previously unseen frames capture the closeness between the McCartneys in the studio, gazing into each other’s eyes and having fun. Responding to negative comments about Linda’s role in the band, the press officer for Wings tells the newspaper they are “passionately, inseparably in love and the question of them doing anything apart was unthinkable”.
Another doyen of the entertainment world, Dick Van Dyke made history this month. The Mary Poppins star, 98, became the oldest Daytime Emmy winner thanks to his role in the US soap opera Days of Our Lives. A video clip went viral of Dyke dancing a merry jig on the red carpet after collecting his award. In 1967 Chris Travis photographed Dyke leaping into the air at the Dorchester hotel as he promoted his new film, Chitty Chitty Bang Bang.
Health warnings were issued this week as temperatures were “set to top 30C”, with the highest temperatures expected in London.
Robert Chandler photographed this London summer scene in 1935. Two ladies caused a stir in the city with their summer sartorial selection.
Summer fashions are always on display at Royal Ascot and 100 years ago Sir Robert Hotung, the Hong-Kong businessman and philanthropist, was photographed exuding style while wearing silk, surrounded by racegoers in customary top hats and tails. His 1956 obituary mourned the passing of the “link between east and west”, a “dignified figure clad in the silken robes of a Chinese gentleman of the old school”. An image from the following year shows Sir James Craig, the former prime minister of Northern Ireland, and Lady Craig ignoring the lady selling heather.
French actress Anouk Aimeé died aged 92. The star of La Dolce Vita was an “elegant, enigmatic and much-married performer who starred in more than 70 films”.
This portrait was taken promoting one of her earliest films, Golden Salamander. Aged 17 she poses alongside her co-star Trevor Howard. The largely unfavourable review of the film in The Times highlights her performance for praise, recognising “an actress in the true sense of the word” displaying a “general air of patience and composure” on screen.
France lost another performer as the singer-songwriter Françoise Hardy died, aged 80.
The singer was admired by the biggest names in 1960s, such as David Bowie and Bob Dylan, who appreciated her “melancholic beauty and wistful lyrics”. These 1964 portraits were taken at Pye studios in London for a profile piece in The Sunday Times. Nicholas Tomalin described her unique style, “a French girl trying to look like an ordinary English girl. She wears tweed skirts and Fair Isle looking jumpers” and “sings sad songs which she writes herself”.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.title: Baillie Gifford book protests hit a soft target, Patrick Harvie says
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.subtitle: Scottish Green co-leader said campaign by Fossil Free Books should have focused on investors rather than defunding literary festivals
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.text:
Patrick Harvie has questioned the tactics of campaigners who wrecked the corporate sponsorship of three Scottish literary festivals.
The Scottish Green co-leader said he had “mixed feelings” about protests aimed at Baillie Gifford, the Edinburgh investment house, over their support for literary events.
Speaking on BBC Scotland’s The Sunday Show, he said he felt campaigners had picked a “soft target instead of a hard one”.
• Why a small band of radicals at Hay is a big problem for the arts
Baillie Gifford has been under fire over its continuing funding of fossil fuel industries, its links with Israel and its history of investing in Russian state mining and banking institutions until President Putin’s full invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The company, which is also a significant backer of the renewables and high-tech sectors, has ended its sweeping financial support for Scottish and other UK literary festivals after threats of protests and boycotts.
A group called Fossil Free Books has led a campaign to highlight Baillie Gifford’s involvement in festivals, including those in Edinburgh, Borders and Wigtown.
Asked how he felt about the campaign, Harvie said: “I have mixed feelings on this, in the way that I do with some of the Extinction Rebellion protests, for example, which impact on people rather than on the big fossil fuel companies.
“The critical thing here is: what is your target? What are you trying to achieve?”
Harvie added: “Now, if the objective of the campaign was to get Baillie Gifford to divest from fossil fuels, from companies that are targeted by Israel, it hasn’t worked.
“The objective should not have been to defund literary festivals. I don’t think that’s what Fossil Free books wanted to see.
“The goal should be to focus on the investors and the investment decisions that they make. That’s a very legitimate goal. The danger here is a campaign that ends up hitting a soft target when it should have been aiming for a hard target.”
Fossil Free Books tweeted on Sunday that Baillie Gifford was “not, and has never been, a sustainable or ethical source of funding for the arts”.
It added: “We call on the UK books industry not to concede to ‘culture wars’ rhetoric” and concluded: “Baillie Gifford must divest.”
The campaign has won support from Friends of the Earth, which issued a post on Twitter/X that said: “Baillie Gifford must turn the page and end its huge investments in weapons of war and fuelling climate breakdown.”
